[USER] User inquired about the differences between frogs and toads and their preferred habitats.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Frogs have smooth, slimy skin while toads have dry, bumpy and warty skin.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Frogs are usually slim and agile while toads are stout and slow-moving.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Frogs are mostly found in or near water such as ponds, lakes, swamps, and other wetlands.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Toads can be found in a wide range of environments such as grasslands, forests, deserts, and rocky areas.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Frogs lay their eggs in clusters, while toads lay them in long strands.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Frogs have longer hind legs compared to their front legs, allowing them to jump and swim efficiently.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Toads have shorter hind legs and mostly walk or slowly hop.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Frogs have a long and sticky tongue for catching insects, while toads have a shorter and less sticky tongue, eating larger prey like worms, snails, and small mammals.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Overall, frogs prefer watery habitats while toads prefer drier areas, with some exceptions.  
[USER] User asked for specific species of frogs and toads that can survive in both wet and dry habitats.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] American toad (Anaxyrus americanus) can tolerate both wet and dry conditions.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Gray treefrog (Hyla versicolor) can survive in both wet and dry environments.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Western toad (Anaxyrus boreas) can tolerate both wet and dry conditions.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Green treefrog (Hyla cinerea) can survive in swamps, wetlands, and drier areas like pine forests and fields.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Fowler's toad (Anaxyrus fowleri) can tolerate both wet and dry conditions.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Even adaptable species have specific habitat requirements and preferences.  
[USER] User inquired about frogs and toads that change color depending on their environment.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Some species of frogs and toads can change color to blend in with their environment, known as "environmental coloration."  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Green treefrog (Hyla cinerea) can change from bright green to brown depending on the surface.
